newsitem.title: USA: FUND VIEW - Weaker yen helps Japan funds in U.S.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Weaker yen helps Japan funds in U.S.

text.p: The weaker yen has helped the performance of some U.S. Japan equity funds in recent days.
According to Lipper Analytical Services, six of the top 10 performing funds for the week ended April 3 were Japan funds, especially ones that hold large multinational Japanese stocks.
Wright EquiFund Japan returned 2.87 percent for the week, finishing in the third spot, and the T. Rowe Price Associates Inc's Japan Fund gained 2.33 percent, finishing in the fifth spot.
The dollar has been pounding the yen in recent sessions. Earlier, week, the dollar surged to its highest level in over four years against the yen, trading as high as 126.52 yen.

Tricia Rothschild, who follows international funds at Morningstar Inc, said the strong dollar/weak yen "certainly puts more of a divergence between the large multinational companies that benefit from a weaker yen and smaller, domestic-oriented stocks that suffer."
Rothschild said some of the weekly gain was attributable to the Tankan survey, which last week showed limited improvement in Japanese corporate confidence.
Khandwala said the drug, cosmetics and healthcare sectors comprised 24 percent of the portfolio, retailers make up 16.4 percent, and electronics companies total 11.6 percent.
Warren said the fund is "fairly concentrated on some of those popular nifty names," especially companies that are big exporters, especially in manufactured electronics."

Top holdings at the price fund include NEC Corp, at 3.5 percent; pharmaceutical maker Sankyo Co Ltd at 3.2 percent; Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd at 3.1 percent; Sony Corp, TDK Corp, and electronics maker Kyocera Corp, each at three percent of the portfolio; and Canon Electronics Inc at 2.7 percent.
Warren asserted that by U.S. valuations, the issues are not too expensive, especially for companies that he termed "world beaters" when it comes to growth.

"They are enjoying pretty strong profit growth, not only by existing product lines, but through new products," Warren said. "These companies are heavy exporters. A weak yen against the dollar is good for their business."
Both Warren and Khandwala said their funds have shied away from Japanese banks, real estate and construction stocks.

With the banks, Warren said, "the underlying business is lousy, and with their bad debt exposure creates a difficult case to buy them." With their problems, Warren believes the bank stocks are "still overvalued."
"They keep on saying that their bad debt...has been written off, but it keeps on appearing, and they keep on making more writeoffs," he said.
He said the banks are also plagued by their inability to consolidate or cut costs as the industry has done in the United States.
In recent weeks, the fund has added to its holdings in mobile telecom company DDI Corp, and Kao Corp, which makes household products.
Cash remains at four percent.

The portfolio has about 140 issues. Warren said the fund has been moving more strongly into small-cap stocks, which now comprise about 15 percent of the portfolio, with the biggest holdings in electronics components and manufacturers.
Warren said he expects the yen to remain at present levels for the near term, rather than weaken further. Warren said the $140 million fund has not recently hedged in currency.

Wright's top holdings include: Seven-Eleven Japan Co Ltd at 6.6 percent; Ito-Yokado Co Ltd at 5.5 percent; Takeda Chemical Industries Ltd at five percent; Sankyo at 4.5 percent; and Kyocera at 4.4 percent.
Rothschild said that smaller-cap Japanese stocks dragged down the average for the 28 Japanese funds in its sector to a 0.43 percent weekly return.

"The Japanese market is very straightforward," said David Warren, co-portfolio manager of the Rowe Price Japan Fund. "You're either in one of about 30 or 40 stocks, the dollar is going up in absolute terms, and everybody is having a good time."
Amit S. Khandwala, who manages the $14 million Wright Japan, said the fund has focused on companies that derive more of their revenues from exports.
